summary.en: Solve twenty original contest-style problems with explicit contracts, efficient input and reusable reasoning patterns.
summary.bn: বিশটা সমস্যা সমাধান করো, ইনপুটের নিয়ম পড়ো আর সময় ও মেমরির হিসাব মিলিয়ে অ্যালগরিদম বেছে নাও।

notes: The Python syntax works on 3.10 and later; optional library releases have their own interpreter requirements.

sections.title: Turn a story into a precise calculation
Read whitespace tokens or preserve a whole line
Choose a pattern and justify its state
Try the case that attacks your assumption
Use familiar syntax with clear limits
Keep a reason beside each shortcut

examples.title: 1. Add signed adjustments
examples.explanationHtml:
Read n (0–100000), followed by exactly n integers from -1000000 to 1000000. Print their sum. Whitespace may span lines.

Start from the additive identity zero. sum naturally handles an empty collection, and negative adjustments need no special branch. Cost: O(n) time and O(n) memory.

examples.title: 2. Share a shuttle fare
examples.explanationHtml:
Read passenger count n (0–1000000000) and positive capacity k (1–1000000000). Print the minimum number of shuttles needed.

Integer ceiling division adds capacity minus one before dividing. A partial last group still needs a shuttle, while zero people need none. Cost: O(1) arithmetic operations.

examples.title: 3. Split a duration
examples.explanationHtml:
Read nonnegative seconds s, at most 1000000000. Print hours, remaining minutes and remaining seconds as three space-separated integers.

divmod gives both quotient and remainder. Convert the remainder rather than converting the original seconds again for every unit. Cost: O(1) arithmetic operations.

examples.title: 4. Validate three sticks
examples.explanationHtml:
Read three integers from -1000000 to 1000000. Print VALID if they can be side lengths of a nondegenerate triangle; otherwise print INVALID.

After sorting positive sides, only the sum of the two smallest needs comparison with the largest. Equality describes a flat shape. Cost: O(1) time and memory.

examples.title: 5. Add digits of a long receipt code
examples.explanationHtml:
Read one nonempty decimal digit string of length at most 100000. Print its digit sum. Leading zeros are allowed.

Read the identifier as text so its length and leading zeros remain available. Iterate characters rather than converting the entire huge integer. Cost: O(d) time and O(d) memory.

examples.title: 6. Find the largest equal packet size
examples.explanationHtml:
Read nonnegative counts a and b, each at most 1000000000. Print their greatest common divisor; define the answer for 0 and 0 as 0.

Replacing a and b with b and the remainder preserves their common divisors. The second number decreases until it reaches zero. Cost: O(log(max(a,b)+1)) division steps.

examples.title: 7. Recognize a prime roll candidate
examples.explanationHtml:
Read n from 0–1000000000. Print PRIME if n is prime and NOT PRIME otherwise.

A composite number has a factor no greater than its square root. The inclusive square bound catches perfect squares such as 49. Cost: O(sqrt(n)) time and O(1) auxiliary memory.

examples.title: 8. Check a mirror token
examples.explanationHtml:
Read one nonempty lowercase ASCII token of length at most 100000. Print YES if it reads the same backward, otherwise NO.

Reversed slicing gives a clear first solution. A pair of inward-moving indices can avoid allocating the reversed string when memory matters. Cost: O(n) time and O(n) extra memory.

practice.title: 9. Choose the most frequent score
practice.statementHtml: Read n (1–100000) then n integers from 0–100. Print the most frequent score and its frequency. Break ties by choosing the smaller score.
hints: Counter records each frequency. The tuple key first favors a larger count, then a smaller value; dictionary insertion order cannot decide ties.

practice.title: 10. List distinct badge numbers
practice.statementHtml: Read n (0–100000) then n integers from 0–1000000000. Print the distinct values in increasing order, separated by spaces; print EMPTY when n is zero.
hints: A set removes duplicate values, then sorting establishes a promised display order. Set iteration alone cannot promise increasing order.

practice.title: 11. Find the first repeated scanner value
practice.statementHtml: Read n (0–100000) then n integers from 0–1000000000. Print the first value whose second appearance is encountered while scanning left to right, or NONE.
hints: Before each iteration, seen holds precisely the earlier values. Membership therefore answers whether this appearance is a repetition.

practice.title: 12. Measure a streak of attendance
practice.statementHtml: Read a binary string of length 0–100000 on one line. Print the longest contiguous run of 1 characters; an empty line has answer 0.
hints: current measures the run ending here, while best records all completed prefixes. A zero resets current without erasing the best earlier streak.

practice.title: 13. Answer repeated inclusive range totals
practice.statementHtml: Read n and q (1–100000 each), n integers of absolute value at most 1000000, then q pairs l r with 1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n. Print one inclusive range sum per line.
hints: prefix[k] totals the first k entries. Subtract the prefix before l from the prefix through r. Preprocessing saves rescanning for every query.

practice.title: 14. Find two distinct tickets totaling a target
practice.statementHtml: Read n (0–100000) and target (-2000000000–2000000000), then n integers from -1000000000 to 1000000000. Print YES if two distinct positions sum to target, otherwise NO.
hints: Sort first. If the smallest available plus the largest is too small, the smallest cannot succeed with any remaining partner. Advance it; apply symmetric reasoning when too large.

practice.title: 15. Merge touching booking intervals
practice.statementHtml: Read n (0–100000), then n closed intervals l r with 0 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ 1000000000. Merge overlapping or touching intervals. Print the merged count, then each merged l r on its own line in increasing order.
hints: Sorting makes every new start no smaller than earlier starts. Only the last merged interval can overlap the next one. Touching means equal endpoints here, not adjacent integer endpoints.

practice.title: 16. Validate nested round and square brackets
practice.statementHtml: Read one line containing only ()[] with length 0–100000. Print YES if brackets are properly nested and NO otherwise. The empty line is valid.
hints: A stack stores unmatched opening brackets. Each closing bracket must match the most recent opening. Checking only the total counts misses crossed nesting.

quiz.prompt: How does the shuttle formula handle thirteen people and capacity six?
quiz.explanation: Integer ceiling division reserves a vehicle for the last incomplete group.

quiz.prompt: Which range sum follows from prefix values [0, 2, 1, 6] for positions two through three?
quiz.explanation: Subtract the prefix before position two from the prefix through position three.

quiz.prompt: Which score wins a frequency tie under the smaller-score rule?
quiz.explanation: The negative count favors larger frequencies, and the value resolves ties.

quiz.prompt: Why can whole-file split input use substantial memory?
options: It streams one byte without storage
It always stores less than readline
It retains the file and many parsed tokens
quiz.explanation: Reading everything is convenient for moderate input; streaming lines may fit large input better.

options: seen contains exactly the values before the current position
quiz.explanation: Membership then detects an earlier appearance.

quiz.prompt: Why initialize a nonempty maximum segment from the first value?
options: All-negative inputs must still choose an actual entry
quiz.explanation: Initializing best to zero would allow the forbidden empty segment.

quiz.prompt: Why does the two-ticket scan require left < right?
options: A position cannot pair with itself
quiz.explanation: Two equal values at different positions are allowed, but reusing one index is not.

quiz.prompt: Which prime-loop boundary includes possible square factors?
quiz.explanation: Perfect squares require checking the square-root divisor itself.

quiz.prompt: What does bisect_left return if every value is below the target?
options: The length of the sorted collection
quiz.explanation: It is an insertion boundary, so it can lie just beyond the last index.

quiz.prompt: Which interval rule merges [1,3] and [3,5] here?
options: All intervals merge regardless of position
quiz.explanation: The task defines touching closed endpoints as mergeable.

quiz.prompt: Why can equal bracket counts still be invalid?
options: Closing order must match the latest opening
An empty string is always invalid
quiz.explanation: Crossed nesting such as ([)] has equal counts but violates stack order.

quiz.prompt: Which step changes prefix-query work from repeated scans to constant-time queries?
options: Convert all values to strings first
Use a set instead of numbers
quiz.explanation: Two prefix lookups and a subtraction answer each query after preprocessing.

examQuestions.question: 17. Count trailing zeros in a factorial: Read n from 0–1000000000. Print the number of decimal trailing zeros in n factorial. Zero factorial equals one.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
Each zero needs a factor ten. Twos are plentiful, so count factors five, including extra contributions from multiples of 25, 125 and later powers. Cost: O(log n) time and O(1) arithmetic storage.

import sys


def main():
    n = int(sys.stdin.buffer.read())
    zeros = 0
    while n:
        n //= 5
        zeros += n
    print(zeros)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

examQuestions.question: 18. Find the best nonempty earnings segment: Read n (1–100000), then n signed integers of absolute value at most 1000000. Print the greatest sum of a nonempty contiguous segment.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
ending is the best nonempty segment ending at this entry. Either extend its predecessor or restart here. Initialize from an actual entry to preserve all-negative answers. Cost: O(n) time and O(n) input memory.

import sys


def main():
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    values = data[1:1 + data[0]]
    ending = best = values[0]
    for value in values[1:]:
        ending = max(value, ending + value)
        best = max(best, ending)
    print(best)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

examQuestions.question: 19. Locate the first eligible sorted value: Read n (0–100000) and target, then n nondecreasing signed integers; all values have absolute value at most 1000000000. Print the zero-based first position whose value is at least target, or n if absent.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
bisect_left locates the boundary between smaller and eligible values. It returns an insertion position, which may equal the collection length; check that before indexing. Cost: O(log n) search time after O(n) input reading.

import sys
from bisect import bisect_left


def main():
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    count, target = data[:2]
    values = data[2:2 + count]
    print(bisect_left(values, target))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

examQuestions.question: 20. Count routes through a small grid: Read rows and columns from 1–30. Start at the top-left cell and move only right or down. Print the number of routes to the bottom-right cell, including one route for a one-cell grid.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
Every inner cell receives routes from above and left. Before updating a column, its stored value belongs to the previous row; its left neighbor already belongs to this row. Cost: O(rows × columns) time and O(columns) memory.

import sys


def main():
    rows, columns = map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split())
    ways = [1] * columns
    for _ in range(1, rows):
        for column in range(1, columns):
            ways[column] += ways[column - 1]
    print(ways[-1])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
